blocks.text: Likewise, to the Abderites of Thrace, who had left their native soil because of the multitude of frogs and mice and were seeking a place to settle, Cassander assigned lands in the farthest borders of Macedonia, as Trogus attests, book 15. Heraclides in the Politiae likewise relates that the Chalcidians settled in Cleonae, ἐν τῷ Ἄθῳ ἐξαναστάντας ἐξ Ἐλυμνίου ὑπὸ μυῶν, οἳ τὰ τ᾽ ἄλλα κατήθιον αὐτῶν, καὶ τὸν σίδηρον [en tō Athō exanastantas ex Elymniou hypo myōn, hoi ta t' alla katēthion autōn, kai ton sidēron], having been driven out of Elymnium on Mount Athos by mice, which devoured not only other things but even iron itself. Others report the same of Gyarus. Pliny, book 8, chapter 29: M. Varro is the authority, etc., that the inhabitants of Gyarus, an island of the Cyclades, were put to flight by mice. And in chapter 57: Theophrastus is the authority that on the island of Cyarus, after they had driven out the inhabitants, they gnawed even iron. Hence Antigonus, Mirabilia, chapter 21: Τῆς δὲ Καρυστίας καὶ τῆς Ἀνδρίας χώρας ἐστὶν πλησίον νῆσος ἡ καλουμένη Γύαρος· ἐνταῦθα οἱ μύες διατρώγουσι τὸν σίδηρον [Tēs de Karystias kai tēs Andrias chōras estin plēsion nēsos hē kaloumenē Gyaros; entautha hoi myes diatrōgousi ton sidēron]. Near Carystia and Andria there is an island named Gyarus, in which mice eat iron. And of the same island Stephanus of Byzantium: Ἀντίγονος δ᾽ ὁ Καρύστιός φησι, ὅτι ἐν ταύτῃ οἱ μύες διατρώγουσι σίδηρον [Antigonos d' ho Karystios phēsi, hoti en tautē hoi myes diatrōgousi sidēron]; and Antigonus of Carystus says that on this island mice [II, 432] eat iron ^{(4)}. Suidas says much the same. Thus the text of Aristotle in the Mirabilia [ch. 24] is corrupt: Ἐν Κύπρῳ τῇ νήσῳ λέγεται τοὺς μέτας τὸν σίδηρον ἐσθίειν [En Kyprō tē nēsō legetai tous metas ton sidēron esthiein]; On the island of Cyprus they say that the metae devour iron. Corrupt also is Aelian, History, book 5, chapter 14: Ἐν τῇ Πάρῳ τῇ νήσῳ Ἀριστοτέλης λέγει μῦς εἶναι, καὶ μέν τοι καὶ γῆν σιτεῖσθαι τὴν σιδηρῶτιν [En tē Parō tē nēsō Aristotelēs legei mys einai, kai men toi kai gēn siteisthai tēn sidērōtin]; Aristotle says that on the island of Paros there are mice which eat iron-bearing earth. For in both places, instead of Κύπρῳ [Kyprō] or Πάρῳ [Parō], one should read Γυάρῳ [Gyarō]; and in the former passage μύας [myas] instead of μέτας [metas], in the latter τὴν σιδηρῖτιν [tēn sidēritin]. What of the fact that the inhabitants of the Troad, whom the Greeks barely subdued in a ten-year war, were forced to yield to this plague and abandoned their homeland? Pliny, book 10, [col. 1019] chapter 65: Very many mice thus spring up in the Troad, and they have already driven out the inhabitants from there. And at Chryse, a city of Mysia, Apollo, angered at the priest Crinis, ἔπεμψεν αὐτοῦ τοῖς ἄγροις μύας, οἵτινες τοὺς καρποὺς ἐλυμαίνοντο [epempsen autou tois agrois myas, hoitines tous karpous elymainonto], sent mice into his fields, which destroyed the crops. So the old Scholiast on Homer, on the word Σμινθεῦ [Smintheu] in book 1 of the Iliad. Of the same kind is what Aelian relates, History, book 12, chapter 5: Τῶν Αἰολέων καὶ τῶν Τρώων τὰ λήϊα πολλὰς μυῶν μυριάδας ἐπελθούσας ἄωρα ὑποκείρειν, καὶ ἀτελῆ τὰ θέρη τοῖς σπείρασιν ὑποφαίνειν [Tōn Aioleōn kai tōn Trōōn ta lēia pollas myōn myriadas epelthousas aōra hypokeirein, kai atelē ta therē tois speirasin hypophainein]; that once very many myriads of mice invaded the crops of the Aeolians and Trojans, cut them down unripe, and made the harvest fruitless for those who had sown ^{(5)}.
